video_title: Databricks CEO: AGI Is Already Here, Why Companies Are Behind, and the Superintelligence Debate
gist: Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi argues AGI (by the 2009-10 AMPLab definition) is already here but enterprises are stuck using AI as 'glorified Google search' plus modest coding gains because of four blockers: context, security, token cost and IP lock-in; he demos Databricks' Genie ontology running the company, explains why Databricks (~$7B run rate, 70-80% growth) is delaying an IPO through the AI transition, and lays out four conditions for recursive self-improvement that he says are not being met, putting the real risk in cyber rather than superintelligence.

themes.theme: Databricks scale, bets and business model

insights.claim: Databricks went from about $1.5 million of revenue in 2015 to a rumored ~$7 billion run rate by August 2026, growing roughly 70-80% year over year.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host); Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Benchmark for the largest private data/AI platform ahead of an eventual IPO and a comp for Snowflake's growth.

insights.claim: Ghodsi attributes Databricks' success to three bets that were contrarian in 2013 - going all-in on cloud, on AI use cases and on open source - with a major analyst firm calling the cloud bet a strategic blunder.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Consensus-defying architecture bets created a multi-year head start that competitors struggled to close.
insights.quote: the only reason we succeeded was because of these bets because they were contrarian

insights.claim: Databricks does not charge for dashboards; it monetizes by being the governed data repository that external agents query, charging consumption on that access, so growth in enterprise agent usage directly drives more queries and revenue acceleration.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Agent adoption is a consumption tailwind for governed data platforms (Databricks, Snowflake) regardless of which model vendor wins.
insights.quote: whenever they have agents and they're using it, then I think we're just in the beginning

insights.claim: The most important enterprise data is data generated by the core product, which sits outside CRM and HR systems - the data Databricks targets.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Value accrues to platforms that hold operational/product data rather than systems-of-record apps.
insights.quote: The most important data any company has is the data on the core product that they have.

insights.claim: Databricks is expanding into adjacent markets, having entered security and marketing, and Ghodsi says it will keep making peripheral product moves.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Databricks increasingly overlaps with security and martech vendors; watch competitive pressure on those categories.

insights.claim: Ghodsi wants Databricks to grow 'way over 100%' rather than 70-80% annually, using internal AI-driven productivity to ship more products and take share.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Signals aggressive reinvestment of AI productivity gains into growth rather than margin.

insights.claim: Ghodsi says AGI by the definition used in Berkeley's AMPLab around 2009-2010 was already achieved last year, and that even if all progress stopped now there is enough intelligence to transform the planet.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Shifts the bottleneck from model capability to deployment and diffusion - favoring enterprise infrastructure over frontier labs.
insights.quote: I think we have all the intelligence we need to uh completely transform the planet.

insights.claim: In daily customer meetings Ghodsi finds enterprises use AI mainly as a 'glorified Google search' via chatbots and for coding, where they see only about 20-30% speedups, with essentially no one running thousands of agents.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Enterprise AI productivity gains are far behind lab narratives; adoption-dependent revenue may ramp slower than expected.
insights.quote: They're just using it as a glorified Google search.

insights.claim: Ghodsi's four blockers to enterprise AI are: missing context (meetings, decisions not captured), cybersecurity/insider-threat risk from giving agents broad data access, exponentially rising token costs without matching revenue growth, and lock-in/IP leakage to model providers.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: A checklist for evaluating enterprise AI vendors: whoever solves context, governance, cost and sovereignty captures spend.

insights.claim: A big bank CEO told Ghodsi the bank will never record its meetings, which Ghodsi says makes it impossible for AI to help because it lacks the decision context.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Regulated incumbents' liability concerns will slow AI value capture in financial services.
insights.quote: If it's not in the meeting, it's useless.

insights.claim: Ghodsi says he knows no company whose revenue began accelerating exponentially in line with its exponentially rising AI token costs, and CFOs eventually push back as opex and COGS rise ahead of earnings calls.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Expect enterprise AI budget scrutiny and demand for cost-routing / open-source model tooling.
insights.quote: is your revenue at your company going up exponentially?

insights.claim: Using Anthropic, OpenAI or similar platforms carries a risk that company data leaks into the next model, and Anthropic is shipping products that compete with partners like Microsoft, including an Excel competitor and Photoshop-like tools.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: Frontier labs moving up the stack threaten application incumbents and push enterprises toward data/intelligence sovereignty.

insights.claim: Above Dunbar's number (~150 people) organizations hit a coordination problem; AI that understands the whole business and org chart can cut latency across the hierarchical tree.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Large incumbents stand to gain most from AI coordination but are slowest to adopt.

insights.claim: Ghodsi sees Block/Square under Jack Dorsey, with its 'company world model', as one of the few firms besides Databricks doing AI-driven company operation at scale, and believes digital natives (10-15 years old) are generally ahead of Fortune 500 incumbents.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Digital-native firms like Block may realize AI operating leverage before legacy peers.
insights.quote: He's calling it the company world model.

insights.claim: Ghodsi expects the enterprise context gap to take 10-15 years to close and GDP to move very slowly, versus labs who expect transformation within 6 months to 2 years.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Temper expectations for near-term macro productivity boosts from AI; diffusion is a decade-long trade.
insights.quote: But I actually think GDP will move very slowly and it's going to take decade for us to actually get through it.

themes.theme: Genie: running Databricks on an ontology

insights.claim: Databricks' Genie product differentiates from other chatbots by continuously building an ontology graph of the company - people, reporting lines, emails, meeting transcripts, Slack, docs, spreadsheets and presentations - and runs 24/7 doing background work.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Enterprise 'company world model' / ontology products are the next battleground (compare Palantir-style ontologies).
insights.quote: The ontology is a graphs that it constantly it's constructing for your company.

insights.claim: Genie analyzed a survey of over 10,000 Databricks employees, showed executive leadership at 88% favorability and the 'action' score at ~60%, and disproved the CFO's hypothesis that poor work-life blend was causing low action scores.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Shows AI replacing week-long data-team analyses for management decisions.

insights.claim: Among Databricks' ~2,000 engineers, code shipped to production follows an L-shaped distribution because the top engineers run automated 'factories', and those top engineers often do not spend more on tokens than others.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: AI developer productivity is highly skewed; smart model routing and open-source models can raise output without raising token spend.
insights.quote: it turns out they're running automated factories, the rest are not.

insights.claim: Token spend can be cut significantly by using open-source models and routing simpler questions to simpler models, for which Databricks sells a product.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Model-routing layers pressure frontier-model pricing and favor cheaper open models.

insights.claim: Databricks measures and aims to reduce the number of 'human blockers' - approvals from legal, finance, marketing or sibling teams - that slow AI-driven work, and auto-routes customer feature requests from meeting transcripts to engineering factories.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: A useful KPI for judging how deeply a company has operationalized AI.
insights.quote: one of our main goals is uh reduce number of human blockers

insights.claim: Ghodsi uses AI to check whether each leader's organization actually follows company culture principles and to compare decision-making culture across regions such as Japan, EMEA and Latam, calling such AI-native operation 'big alpha' while it is not yet diffused.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Early adopters of AI management tooling may enjoy a temporary competitive edge.
insights.quote: But right now, this is big alpha.

insights.claim: Ghodsi says Databricks will go public, but is staying private during the AI transition because public-market volatility effectively cuts employee pay, demoralizes CEOs and distracts from long-term building.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Do not expect a near-term Databricks IPO; large AI-era private companies may stay private longer.
insights.quote: We will go public. We are going to be public, but right now, I think during this transition period of AI, there's just too much up and down

insights.claim: Databricks runs annual employee tender offers and has raised roughly $20-30 billion, and the money set aside for tenders has never been fully used because most employees are bullish.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Undersubscribed tenders signal strong insider conviction in valuation.
insights.quote: they never use up all of it. So most employees are bullish.

insights.claim: Predictable liquidity lets Databricks do billion-dollar acquisitions with equity, and employees asked how much to sell typically choose only ~5% once they compound 70-80% growth.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Private equity currency remains effective for M&A when secondary liquidity is reliable.

insights.claim: Ghodsi lists public-company advantages as access to capital and quarterly marketing events, versus the heavy lift of organizing private tenders each year.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Framework for weighing late-stage IPO timing.

insights.claim: Ghodsi argues that AI writing 98% of code does not constitute recursive self-improvement, since automating the last 2% does not matter.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Counters fast-takeoff narratives driving AI-risk policy and lab valuations.
insights.quote: Just because 98% of the code is being written by AI, we don't have RSI. If it automates the last 2%, who cares?

insights.claim: Ghodsi's four conditions for RSI: each training run must get super-linearly faster, use fewer resources, improve accuracy generally across all tasks, and do all three continuously in a loop (e.g., next model in 3 months, then 1 month, then 2 weeks at falling cost).
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: A concrete checklist to monitor whether a takeoff flywheel is actually forming.

insights.claim: Ghodsi says the RSI flywheel does not exist today: models take longer to train, scaling laws require ~10x compute for linear gains, and labs rely on manual domain-by-domain reinforcement-learning data from vendors like Mercor.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Continued dependence on compute and expert-data vendors supports AI capex and data-labeling businesses.
insights.quote: That flywheel doesn't exist right now.

insights.claim: Ghodsi believes AI coding automation is causing an existential crisis in Silicon Valley among lifelong coders, which feeds superintelligence fears.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Explains sentiment-driven AI-risk narratives rather than evidence-based ones.

insights.claim: Ghodsi puts existential AI risk close to zero, saying he sees no evidence of RSI among San Francisco labs, while the host notes Dario's claim that cancer and Alzheimer's could be gone within 10 years and Ghodsi says human trials make timing uncertain (10 to 50 years).
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Skepticism of both doom and utopian timelines; drug-discovery AI value is real but gated by trials.
insights.quote: But I for me, that risk is, you know, close to zero.

themes.theme: Cyber is the real AI risk

insights.claim: Ghodsi calls cyber the biggest current AI risk because attackers can launch thousands of agents and need only one to succeed, while defenders must be secure 100% of the time.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Sustained demand for AI-native security and agent monitoring products.

insights.claim: Ghodsi expects the cyber problem to reach a steady state because new AI-written code is being scanned for vulnerabilities and legacy code can be rewritten or shadow-patched, leaving only a finite set of latent bugs to fix.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Near-term boom in code scanning and legacy rewrite spend, with eventual normalization.
insights.quote: there's only a finite number of vulnerabilities in the code

insights.claim: Ghodsi predicts more code will be written in the next 12 months than in all prior history.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Tailwind for code security, dev tooling and compute consumption.
insights.quote: In the next 12 months, we're going to write more code than ever in the history of mankind

insights.claim: Databricks sells a cybersecurity product (rendered 'Likewatch' in captions) that uses automated agents to detect intrusions and monitor customers' agents.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Databricks is now a competitor in security analytics/SIEM.

insights.claim: Regeneron used Databricks to find the gene responsible for chronic liver disease, and Databricks has now trained a model with Merck called Teddy (Transformer Enabled Drug Discovery) that predicts gene regulatory networks to distinguish causal genes from reactive ones.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi
insights.so_what: Pharma is adopting transformer models for target identification; watch Merck/Regeneron pipelines.
insights.quote: This genome is just reacting to it. So don't target it for a drug.
